title: systemctl status
task: Check whether a service is running and read its last log lines
privilege: none for status; `systemctl --failed` needs no privilege
changes: No. Read-only.
commands:
systemctl status sshd
systemctl status sshd --no-pager
systemctl --failed
systemctl is-active sshd; echo $?
explain: `status` is for humans: it prints the loaded unit, whether it is enabled, the PID, uptime, the cgroup, and roughly the last ten log lines.
`--no-pager` stops `less` taking over. Essential over SSH and in any script or capture.
`is-active` prints one word and sets the exit code: 0 active, 3 inactive, 4 unknown. That is what you want in automation.
example: On a lab VM, `systemctl status sshd --no-pager` normally shows `Active: active (running)` with a `Main PID:` line. If it shows `Active: failed`, scroll up — the last few log lines above the status block are usually the reason.
output:
# systemctl status sshd --no-pager
● sshd.service - OpenSSH server daemon
   Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service; enabled; vendor preset: enabled)
   Active: active (running) since Sat 2026-10-10 09:14:22 BST; 2min 11s ago
     Docs: man:sshd(8) man:sshd_config(5)
   Main PID: 1184 (sshd)
      Tasks: 1 (limit: 61440)
   Memory: 5.1M
verify: systemctl is-active sshd && systemctl is-enabled sshd && echo OK

errors.message: Unit sshd.service could not be found.
errors.means: The package is not installed. On RHEL the unit name is `sshd`, not `ssh` — this is the single most common cause of a learner believing SSH is missing when the package is `openssh-server`.
errors.fix: rpm -q openssh-server || sudo dnf install -y openssh-server

errors.message: Failed to connect to bus: No such file or directory
errors.means: systemd is not PID 1, so you are in a container. `systemctl` will not work at all here.
errors.fix: podman run ... --systemd  (or use a VM)

sources.title: systemd.service(8) / RHEL 10 docs — Using systemd units

title: systemctl enable --now
task: Start a service now and make it start at every boot
changes: Yes. Starts the service and writes symlinks under /etc/systemd/system.
undo: systemctl disable --now NAME   (stops it and removes the boot-time symlinks)
risks: If you enable and start a service you did not mean to — a database, a file server — it becomes reachable on the network immediately.
commands:
sudo systemctl enable --now sshd
systemctl cat sshd | head -5
systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled | grep sshd
explain: `start` is runtime only and is forgotten at reboot. `enable` is boot-time only and does not start anything now. `--now` does both in one step, which is almost always what an administrator actually wants.
You can verify the boot-time half without trusting the message: `systemctl is-enabled sshd` must print `enabled`.
`systemctl cat` shows the unit file systemd actually loaded, including any drop-ins merged over the package default.
example: Installing a package does not start it on RHEL in most cases. `sudo dnf install -y httpd` leaves httpd installed and stopped. The step people forget is `enable --now`.
verify:
systemctl is-enabled sshd
systemctl is-active sshd

errors.message: Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/sshd.service → /usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service
errors.means: This is success, not an error. `enable` prints the symlink it created. Do not be alarmed by the arrow; it points at the vendor file, which is correct.

errors.message: Failed to enable unit: Unit file sshd.service does not exist.
errors.means: The package is not installed. `enable` cannot enable a unit that does not exist.
errors.fix: sudo dnf install -y openssh-server && sudo systemctl enable --now sshd

title: journalctl -u UNIT
task: Read the log messages for one service
privilege: none for your own units; some messages are root-only
changes: No. Read-only.
commands:
journalctl -u sshd -b --no-pager
journalctl -u sshd --since '30 minutes ago' --no-pager
journalctl -xe
journalctl -u nginx -p err -b --no-pager
explain: `-u` restricts to one unit. `-b` means "since this boot", which is almost always what you want — without it you are reading last week's crash too.
`-x` adds explanatory text and `-e` jumps to the end, so the newest (and usually most relevant) lines are visible immediately.
`-p err` filters by priority. Priorities are `emerg alert crit err warning notice info debug`, and `-p err` means err **and worse**.
example: A service shows `Active: failed` in `systemctl status`. The cause is almost always in the last lines of `journalctl -u NAME -b`, not in the status block itself.

errors.message: No journal files were found. Run 'journalctl --flush' to rotate journals.
errors.means: The journal directory is empty — logs are not persistent, usually because /var/log/journal does not exist so everything went to a volatile store.
errors.fix: sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal && sudo systemd-catalog-files  # then restart the service

errors.message: Hint: You are currently not seeing messages from the users of the system.
errors.means: Normal when running as a non-root user. You are seeing the system journal only.
errors.fix: sudo journalctl -u sshd -b --no-pager

title: ss -lntup
task: See what is listening, on which address, and which process owns the port
privilege: root shows process names for sockets you do not own
changes: No. Read-only.
commands:
ss -lntup
ss -lntup 'sport = :22'
ss -lntp state established
ss -lntup | grep -E 'nginx|sshd'
explain: ss replaces netstat on modern RHEL. `-l` listening, `-n` numeric (skip the slow reverse DNS), `-t` TCP, `-u` UDP, `-p` process.

The address column is the most useful part of this output. `0.0.0.0:22` means reachable from every interface; `127.0.0.1:8080` means only from this machine. A service "not working from another PC" is very often bound to localhost.
Appending a filter such as `'sport = :22'` is much more reliable than grep when a port number appears inside an address.
example: You started Apache and cannot reach it from your laptop. `ss -lntup` shows `:::80` and `:::443` — that is fine. If it showed `127.0.0.1:80` instead, that would explain it exactly.

errors.message: netstat: command not found (when using the old tool)
errors.means: netstat is not installed on a minimal RHEL 10 image. That is expected, not a fault. `ss` covers everything netstat did.
errors.fix: ss -lntup    # or: sudo dnf install -y iproute  (ss ships in iproute, usually already present)

title: dnf
task: Install, remove, update and query packages
changes: Yes. Changes installed packages on disk.
undo: dnf history undo <ID>   (dnf keeps a transaction log — this is the real undo)
risks: A major-version update can pull a new kernel and change service behaviour. Never run a blanket `dnf update` on a production server without a plan and a rollback window.
commands:
dnf search nginx
dnf info nginx
sudo dnf install -y nginx
rpm -q nginx
dnf history list | head
sudo dnf history undo <ID>
explain: RHEL 10 ships **dnf4** as `dnf`. Some Fedora and derivative builds have moved to dnf5, which prints differently and parses some options differently — check `dnf --version` before copying a command from a blog.
`dnf history` is the feature most learners never find and it is the answer to "I broke something with an update". Every transaction has an ID and `dnf history undo ID` reverses it.
`dnf install` resolves dependencies for you. Reach for `rpm -i` only when you are deliberately installing a locally-built .rpm and you understand what it will not resolve for you.
example: `dnf history undo 42` rolls back the whole transaction, including packages that were upgraded as a side effect. It is the fastest correct recovery from a bad `dnf update`.

errors.message: Error: Failed to download metadata for repo 'baseos'
errors.means: No working mirror, or a proxy/DNS problem. Nothing to do with the package name.
errors.fix:
sudo dnf clean all && sudo dnf makecache
# still failing: check connectivity and DNS — ping the mirror, then cat /etc/resolv.conf

errors.message: Error: package nginx is already installed
errors.means: It is installed but not started, or not enabled. Installing again does nothing useful.
errors.fix: sudo systemctl enable --now nginx

title: ausearch -m avc
task: Find out whether SELinux blocked something
changes: No. Read-only.
commands:
getenforce
ausearch -m avc -ts recent
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent | tail -30
sestatus
explain: AVC = Access Vector Cache. Every SELinux denial produces one. It names the process's type, the target's type, and the exact permission that was refused — which is what you need, because it tells you what to relabel rather than guessing.
`-ts recent` limits to the current time window. Without a time bound an old denial from last week will be the first thing you read.
Never fix a SELinux problem by setting it to permissive and moving on. Use the boolean or the label fix shown in the denial — permissive teaches you nothing and leaves the system vulnerable.
example: A web server can read `/srv/www` but Apache returns 403. `ausearch -m avc -ts recent` shows `denied { read } for ... scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:default_t:s0`. The fix is to give the files the right label, not to disable SELinux.

errors.message: nothing matches (no output at all)
errors.means: Either there was no denial in that window, or auditd is not running and denials are not being recorded.
errors.fix: systemctl is-active auditd || sudo systemctl enable --now auditd

title: firewall-cmd
task: Inspect and change which ports firewalld allows
changes: Yes, unless you pass --runtime or --permanent and forget to reload.
undo: sudo firewall-cmd --remove-port=443/tcp   (or remove the rich rule you added)
risks: Opening a port exposes the service beyond the machine. Removing the SSH port rule while connected over SSH will lock you out on the next reload.
commands:
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=443/tcp --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --list-ports
explain: firewalld keeps two rule sets. The **runtime** rules apply now and are lost on reload or reboot. The **permanent** rules are the stored config and only apply after `--reload` or a reboot. Passing `--permanent` alone changes nothing live, which is the single most common firewalld misunderstanding.
`--add-service=http` is shorthand for the predefined service definition (port + protocol + any default). Prefer it over `--add-port` when a service is already known to firewalld.
Zone matters: a network interface is bound to exactly one zone, and only that zone's rules apply to connections arriving on it.
example: You run `firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent`, test, and it does not work. This is expected: permanent rules are not live. Add it at runtime too, or reload.

errors.message: FirewallD is not running
errors.means: firewalld is stopped, so nothing is filtering. Another firewall layer (nftables rules, cloud security group) may be.
errors.fix: sudo systemctl enable --now firewalld

errors.message: Error: ZONE_CONFLICT: 'br0' already bound to zone 'X'
errors.means: An interface can only be in one zone. Use --change-interface instead of --add-interface.
errors.fix: sudo firewall-cmd --zone=X --change-interface=br0 --permanent && sudo firewall-cmd --reload

title: nmcli connection
task: Inspect and change network interface configuration
changes: Yes. Modifies the connection profile and can drop the network.
undo: Keep a console session open, or record the previous profile with `nmcli con show NAME` first. Changes to a connection started with `autoconnect no` are not applied until you do `nmcli con up NAME`.
risks: Changing the address on the interface you are connected through will drop your SSH session immediately. Over a remote connection, always schedule the change with `nmcli con up` in the background, or use a two-minute revert timer.
commands:
nmcli device status
nmcli connection show
nmcli connection show 'System eth0'
sudo nmcli connection modify 'System eth0' ipv4.method manual \
     ipv4.addresses 192.0.2.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.0.2.1 \
     ipv4.dns '192.0.2.53' ipv4.dns-search example.lan
nmcli -p connection show --active
explain: NetworkManager stores settings as **connection profiles**, not as files per interface. The profile name (`System eth0`) is what you modify and activate; the device name (`eth0`) is just the plug it is currently on.

`ipv4.method` is the switch that matters: `auto` = DHCP, `manual` = static, `disabled` = no IPv4. Most "my server has no IP" problems are a profile still set to `auto` on a network with no DHCP server.
There are two ways to set an IP: `ipv4.addresses` on the profile (persistent) or `ip addr add` on the device (lost at reboot). Always use the profile.
example:
To make a change reversible over SSH, schedule the activation and a forced revert:
  sudo nmcli con down 'System eth0' && sudo nmcli con up 'System eth0'
  (sleep 120; sudo nmcli con mod 'System eth0' ipv4.method auto; sudo nmcli con up 'System eth0') &
If the new address works, the revert is still scheduled — cancel it with `kill %1`.
verify:
ip -br address show
ip route
nmcli -f IN-USE,NAME,DEVICE connection show --active

errors.message: Error: Failed to add IPv4 address: File exists
errors.means: The address is already on that device. You are adding rather than replacing.
errors.fix: sudo nmcli connection modify 'System eth0' ipv4.addresses '192.0.2.10/24'   # no comma = replace the list

errors.message: Connection activation failed: No suitable device found
errors.means: The profile's `connection.interface-name` does not match any device. Common after a hardware change or in a VM where the NIC name differs.
errors.fix: nmcli device status   # then correct interface-name, or delete the constraint entirely

title: show ip interface brief
task: See every interface, its IP address, status and protocol state
where: Cisco IOS / IOS XE privileged EXEC
changes: No. Read-only.
commands:
enable
show ip interface brief
explain: Two status columns matter and people conflate them. **Status** is the physical/line protocol up-down. **Protocol** is whether the software protocol is up (has an IP, is not shut).
`administratively down` in the Status column means someone issued `shutdown` on the interface. That is a configuration fact, not a hardware fault.
This is the first command for any "it is not working" question on a switch or router. It answers: do I have an address, and is the port actually enabled.
example: On an unconfigured access switch, Gi0/1 might read `down  down  unassigned` — status down because nothing is plugged in, protocol down because there is no IP. That is normal and not an error on a Layer-2 access port.
verify:
show ip interface brief
show interfaces status

errors.message: % Invalid input detected at '^' marker.
errors.means: You are in the wrong mode. `show` is a privileged-EXEC command, not a config command.
errors.fix: enable      # then run it again

sources.title: Cisco IOS Command Reference — show ip interface brief

title: show running-config interface
task: Read the exact configuration of one interface
where: Cisco IOS / IOS XE privileged EXEC
changes: No. Read-only.
commands:
enable
show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/1
show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1
show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 switchport
explain: Configuration tells you what is *supposed* to be true; `show interfaces` tells you what is *actually* happening (rate, errors, resets, queue drops). You need both before you blame hardware.
The line-protocol-down line in `show interfaces` usually names the reason outright: `err-disabled`, `access VLAN does not exist`, `no such interface`, or `administratively down`.
`show interfaces <x> switchport` is the one to run when a port is up but a client cannot get an address. It shows mode, VLAN, and whether it is a trunk.
example: A client is on Gi0/3 and gets no DHCP offer. `show interfaces gi0/3 switchport` shows `Administrative Mode: access` and `Operational Mode: down` — the port is shut, so nothing can pass.
verify:
show interfaces status
show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 counters errors

errors.message: % Invalid input detected
errors.means: On many platforms the short form `show run int Gi0/1` works but `Gi0/1` must match the actual name. Catalyst 2960-X uses `GigabitEthernet0/1`; a Catalyst 9300 stack member may use `GigabitEthernet1/0/1`.
errors.fix: show interfaces status | include Gi0/1   # find the real name first

sources.title: Cisco Catalyst 2960-X Series Switch Command Reference

title: vlan database / configure terminal
task: Create a VLAN and put an access port into it
where: Cisco IOS privileged EXEC then config
platform: IOS 15.x (IOS XE 17.x on Catalyst 9000 uses global config)
changes: Yes. Creates a VLAN and moves the port into it.
undo: The port keeps the VLAN until reassigned. Removing the VLAN: `no vlan 20` (from vlan database). Removing the last port in a VLAN deletes it automatically on most platforms.
risks: Moving a live port between VLANs drops its connectivity for a second or two. Never change a port a user is actively on without saying so.
commands:
enable
vlan database
 vlan 20
  name USERS
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/3
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
 spanning-tree portfast
end
write memory
show vlan brief
show interfaces status
explain: On a Catalyst 2960-class switch, VLANs are created in `vlan database` mode, **not** in `configure terminal`. On Catalyst 9000 running IOS XE, the modern form `configure terminal` then `vlan 20` is used. Knowing which platform you are on is the whole point of this entry.
`switchport mode access` is required in addition to `switchport access vlan 20`. The access VLAN does not take effect on a trunk port.
`write memory` (or `copy running-config startup-config`) persists. In Packet Tracer and in a live switch, skipping it is why the VLAN vanished after a reload in the lab.
example: Two ports in the same VLAN can reach each other; two ports in different VLANs cannot, without routing. If a client is isolated in its own VLAN, check the access VLAN on both the port and the uplink port on the other switch.
verify:
show vlan brief
show interfaces gi0/3 switchport
show mac address-table interface gi0/3

errors.message: % Invalid input detected at '^' marker.
errors.means: You typed `vlan 20` in `configure terminal` on a 2960-class switch.
errors.fix: enable → vlan database → vlan 20 → name USERS → exit

errors.message: % Default VLAN 1 may not be deleted.
errors.means: VLAN 1 is the default and always exists.
errors.fix: Choose a different VLAN number.

sources.title: Cisco Catalyst 2960-X Series Switch Command Reference

title: ping / traceroute
task: Test reachability and find where a path breaks
changes: No. Read-only.
commands:
enable
ping 10.0.0.1 repeat 5
ping 10.0.0.1 source 10.0.0.9
traceroute 8.8.8.8
show ip route
explain: `repeat 5` stops Cisco ping from running forever — always use it over a console, or you will have to interrupt.

`source` matters more than people expect. A ping from a router uses the IP of the interface the traffic exits. If a server is allowed to be pinged only from one address and the router picks another, you get a false negative.

Traceroute answers a routing question, not a reachability question. ICMP time-exceeded responses are frequently filtered, so `*` in the middle of a trace is not by itself a fault — look at the last responding hop and confirm with pings.
example: A path works from your PC but not from the server. Before touching the firewall, compare `ping <host> source <server-ip>` from the router — that isolates routing from the host itself.

errors.message: ..... 100% loss (5 echo requests sent, 0 received)
errors.means: No ICMP reply. This is **not** proof the host is down — ICMP is frequently rate-limited or blocked. Check `show ip route` for a route to the destination first.
errors.fix:
show ip route <destination>
show arp | include <next-hop>

errors.message: Type escape sequence to abort.
errors.means: Normal. You can interrupt the command.

title: /ip address print
task: List every IP address assigned to the router
changes: No. Read-only.
commands:
/ip/address/print
/ip/address/print detail
/ip/interface/print
/ip/interface/print type=ether
explain: RouterOS uses a **menu path**, not a Linux-style command. The leading `/` means "jump to this menu"; everything before the last `/` navigates and the last word is the operation. Typing `/ip/address/print` is equivalent to pressing `/ip address` then `print`.
`print` shows the set. `print detail` shows every field including the disabled flag and comment — which is often where the answer is.
In RouterOS 7, `/interface/bridge/port` and `/interface/ethernet` are separate menus; in v6 they were all under `/interface`. This is the main practical difference worth remembering.
example: An interface with a correct address shows `D` for dynamic in the flags column. If you expected a static address and see D, someone (or the DHCP client) created it dynamically and it may change.

errors.message: unknown command
errors.means: A typo, or a menu path that does not exist in your version. RouterOS 6 and 7 differ on `/interface`.
errors.fix: Press `/` then Tab to browse the menu tree. Or `/interface/print` to see what exists.

errors.message: failure: address already exists
errors.means: That address is already assigned to another interface.
errors.fix: /ip/address/print   # find who holds it

title: /ip firewall filter
task: Add a rule that allows or denies traffic and see what is already there
changes: Yes. Changes packet filtering immediately, with no confirmation prompt.
undo: /ip/firewall/filter/remove <number>   or remove by comment: ... where comment="..."
risks: A filter rule that drops established connections can cut your own management session. Read the existing rules with `print` before you add anything, and keep a way back in (WinBox from the LAN, or the console port).
commands:
/ip/firewall/filter/print
/ip/firewall/filter/add chain=input action=accept \
   protocol=icmp comment="accept ping to router"
/ip/firewall/filter/add chain=input action=drop \
   in-interface-list=!WAN connection-state=established,related \
   comment="default drop invalid"
/ip/firewall/filter/print stats
explain: MikroTik's model is **three separate chains**: `input` (traffic to the router itself), `forward` (traffic passing through it), and `output` (traffic from the router). Choosing the wrong chain is the single most common reason a rule appears to do nothing.
Order is evaluated top to bottom, first match wins, exactly like an ACL. Put accepts above drops.
The default configuration ships with rules allowing established/related through `forward`. Adding a drop in the wrong place silently overrides them.

In RouterOS 7, the modern drop-in replacement for a bare port filter is the **address list + connection tracking** pattern, but `filter` is still the right tool for core filtering and is what exams and most lab work expect.
example: To see whether a rule is actually matching anything, add `stats` and re-run `print` — the `packets` column shows the hit count. A rule with zero hits after a test is not doing what you think.

errors.message: failure: already have such address
errors.means: Duplicate address-list entry.
errors.fix: /ip/firewall/address-list/print   # remove the old entry first

errors.message: Rule matched but nothing happens to the client
errors.means: Usually the rule is in the wrong chain, or a NAT rule is required in addition to a filter rule. Filtering without masquerading drops outbound replies.
errors.fix: /ip/firewall/nat/print   # confirm a masquerade or srcnat rule exists on the WAN interface

title: /ip dhcp-server network
task: Define and enable the DHCP scope the router hands out
changes: Yes. Starts handing out addresses.
risks: A DHCP scope whose gateway or DNS points somewhere wrong produces clients that appear to work but cannot reach anything. Always check `network=` before enabling.
commands:
/ip/dhcp-server/network/print
/ip/dhcp-server/network/add name=LAN address=10.10.20.1/24 \
   gateway=10.10.20.1 dns-server=10.10.20.1
/ip/dhcp-server/add name=lan-dhcp interface=bridge-lan \
   address-pool=lan-pool lease-time=1h disabled=no
/ip/dhcp-server/print
/ip/dhcp-server/lease/print
/ip/pool/print
explain: DHCP needs four separate pieces and a beginner usually configures three: a **pool** (the address range), a **network** (gateway, DNS, domain, netmask), and a **server** (which interface it answers on). The server also needs a `lease-time`.
The gateway is usually the router's own address on that bridge. If clients get an address but no route out, this is why.
`/ip/dhcp-server/lease/print` is the diagnostic command. No leases while a client is failing means the client never reached the server; leases with the wrong gateway means the scope is misconfigured.
In RouterOS 7 the DHCP server is under `/ip/dhcp-server` with options under `/ip/dhcp-server/network/<name>/set` — not the older v6 `/ip/dhcp-server/network` combined layout. Check your version.
example: Client says 'Unable to obtain an IP address'. If DHCP is on the bridge and the client is on a bridge port, it works. If the client is on a physical port not in the bridge, it never sees the DHCP offer — that is a bridge membership problem, not a DHCP problem.

errors.message: failure: could not add address ... already exists
errors.means: The pool overlaps the network range or the bridge address.
errors.fix: /ip/pool/print   # make the pool exclude the gateway address

errors.message: Client gets 169.254.x.x
errors.means: The client fell back to APIPA, meaning it never got an offer at all.
errors.fix: Check the DHCP server is enabled, is bound to the right interface, and that a firewall rule is not dropping UDP 67.

title: ipconfig /all
task: See the full network configuration of every adapter
changes: No. Read-only.
commands:
ipconfig /all
ipconfig /renew
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /flushdns
nslookup example.lan
explain: `/all` is the useful one. Plain `ipconfig` only shows address, mask and gateway; `/all` adds DHCP status, DNS servers, MAC, and the adapter description — the MAC and description are what you need when a switch port shows the wrong device.
A `169.254.x.x` address means DHCP failed and Windows self-assigned. That is a symptom, not a cause: either no DHCP server on that segment, or the link is down.
`ipconfig /flushdns` is the first thing to try for "it worked yesterday" name-resolution problems, and it is harmless.
In PowerShell, `ipconfig` is still an external command; `Clear-DnsClientCache` and `Get-DnsClientServerAddress` are the native equivalents.
example: A Windows 11 client on a network with DHCP shows `DHCP Enabled: Yes`. If it shows `No`, someone set a static address. That single line explains a lot of otherwise mysterious failures.

errors.message: Media State ... Media disconnected
errors.means: The adapter has no carrier — cable, switch port, or the adapter is disabled.
errors.fix: Check the cable and the switch port LED first. Nothing above the physical layer will work until this is fixed.

errors.message: The requested operation requires elevation
errors.means: You are in a standard prompt and the command needs administrator rights.
errors.fix: Start → Terminal (Administrator)

title: bcdedit
task: Inspect and change Windows boot options such as safe mode
changes: Yes. Modifies the boot configuration, which can prevent Windows from starting.
undo: bcdedit /deletevalue {current} safeboot    — or from the recovery console, bcdedit /set {default} safeboot no
risks: Setting the wrong value can leave a machine unbootable. Always record `bcdedit /enum {current}` output before changing anything, and prefer `/set {current}` over `/set {default}` when the machine has multiple entries.
explain: Safe mode loads a minimal driver set. It is the standard next step for a machine that will not boot, because it distinguishes 'a driver is broken' from 'Windows itself is broken'.
`{current}` targets the boot entry this operating system was started from. `{default}` targets the entry Windows will use next. On a machine with multiple boot entries these are different.
`bcdedit` must run in an elevated prompt. A normal prompt gives 'The requested operation requires elevation'.
The modern equivalent for most people is holding Shift while clicking Restart, which builds the same environment from the recovery menu without typing anything.
example: Windows updates repeatedly fail with a rollback: enter safe mode, uninstall the last update or driver, remove the safeboot value, and reboot.

errors.message: Access is denied.
errors.means: Not elevated.
errors.fix: Run the terminal as Administrator

errors.message: The boot entry is not found
errors.means: The GUID in braces does not exist on this machine — usually {default} vs {current} mismatch after an OS upgrade.
errors.fix: bcdedit /enum   # list all entries and their identifiers

title: DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
task: Repair a corrupted Windows component store, then verify system files
changes: Yes. Rewrites system component files. Needs internet access to fetch replacements.
undo: No direct undo. Take a restore point or full backup first.
risks: On a machine that boots but misbehaves, run these before anything destructive. On a machine that will not boot, they need WinRE.
commands:
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /CheckHealth
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /ScanHealth
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
sfc /scannow
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /AnalyzeComponentStore
explain: Run DISM **first**, then SFC. DISM repairs the source of the component files from which SFC copies replacements; running SFC first on a corrupted store often fails with 'found corrupt files but was unable to fix some of them'.
`/CheckHealth` is a fast, near-instant check that answers 'is the component store corrupt at all'. Run it before the 10-minute `/RestoreHealth`.
`/RestoreHealth` normally pulls replacement files from Windows Update, so it needs a working network connection and working TLS. Behind a proxy it fails with 0x800f081f.

After a successful DISM, `sfc /scannow` replaces the actual system files. Its output is one of: no integrity violations; repaired; or could not repair — which means the underlying problem is not a file problem.
example: A Windows 11 machine that blue-screens on boot, or where random DLLs are missing, is fixed by DISM then SFC about nine times out of ten. Record the exact DISM exit code: 0 is success, 3010 is success but a reboot is needed.

errors.message: Error: 0x800f081f — The source files could not be found.
errors.means: Windows Update could not supply the replacement files. Common on a machine with no internet, a broken cert store, or a hard-coded bad WSUS setting.
errors.fix: Test connectivity to Windows Update. Then check: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate"  # a PolicyURL pointing at a dead WSUS is the usual culprit

errors.message: Windows Resource Protection found corrupt files but was unable to fix some of them.
errors.means: SFC ran before DISM, or DISM itself failed. Do not keep re-running SFC.
errors.fix: Run DISM /RestoreHealth, then sfc /scannow again.

title: Install-WindowsFeature
task: Install a Windows Server role or feature from the command line
changes: Yes. Installs roles, creates the corresponding services, and can promote a server to a domain controller.
risks: Promoting to a domain controller is not cleanly reversible: the promotion writes to the AD database and creates the NTDS settings. Demoting is possible but is a documented, careful procedure, not a rollback.
commands:
Get-WindowsFeature
Get-WindowsFeature -Name AD-Domain-Services
Install-WindowsFeature -Name AD-Domain-Services -IncludeManagementTools
Install-WindowsFeature -Name RSAT-AD-Tools
Install-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services,DHCP -IncludeManagementTools
Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object Installed -eq $true
explain: The feature names are exact strings and case does not matter but spelling does. Common ones: `AD-Domain-Services` (Active Directory), `DHCP`, `DNS`, `FileServices`, `FS-FileServer`, `RSAT-AD-Tools` (the AD PowerShell tools, which are NOT installed by default and which you will need).
`-IncludeManagementTools` installs the matching MMC snap-in. Without it the feature works but you get no graphical manager, and the default is to omit it — a frequent surprise.
`RSAT-AD-Tools` is the one people forget. `Get-ADUser` fails with 'The term is not recognised' until it is installed, which people misdiagnose as 'PowerShell is broken'.
`Install-WindowsFeature` handles dependencies. Installing `AD-Domain-Services` pulls in `AD-Domain-Services-Deployment` and the DNS server role automatically.
Installing a role does not configure it. After installing DHCP or DNS you still have to create the scope or the zone — that is the separate, more instructive step.
example: A first domain controller: Install-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services -IncludeManagementTools, then Install-ADDSForest with `-DomainName` and `-InstallDns` to create DNS in the same pass.
verify:
Get-WindowsFeature -Name AD-Domain-Services | Select-Object Name, InstallState
Get-Service -Name NTDS, Dhcp, DNS

errors.message: The term 'Get-ADUser' is not recognized
errors.means: The AD PowerShell module is not installed. Windows Server does not include it by default.
errors.fix: Install-WindowsFeature RSAT-AD-Tools

errors.message: Install-WindowsFeature : Operation is not supported on this platform
errors.means: You are on a client SKU, or the feature is not valid for this installation type (e.g. a container).
errors.fix: Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object Name -like 'AD*'   # confirm what this SKU supports

sources.title: Microsoft Learn — AD DS Deployment Overview

title: Add-DhcpServerv4Scope
task: Create a DHCP IPv4 scope with a pool, options and a reservation
privilege: Administrator, or a DHCP admin group
changes: Yes. Starts handing out addresses in the scope.
risks: A scope with a bad router (option 3) or DNS (option 6) hands out leases that look perfect and cannot reach anything. Verify both before you enable it broadly.
commands:
Get-DhcpServerv4Scope
Add-DhcpServerv4Scope -ScopeAddress 10.20.30.0 -PrefixLength 24 \
  -Name 'Sales' -StartRange 10.20.30.100 -EndRange 10.20.30.199
Set-DhcpServerv4ScopeOptionValue -ScopeId 10.20.30.0 -OptionId 3 -Value '10.20.30.1'
Set-DhcpServerv4ScopeOptionValue -ScopeId 10.20.30.0 -OptionId 6 -Value '10.20.30.53'
Add-DhcpServerv4Reservation -ScopeId 10.20.30.0 -IPAddress 10.20.30.50 -ClientId 'AABBCCDDEEFF'
Set-DhcpServerv4Scope -ScopeId 10.20.30.0 -State Active
Get-DhcpServerv4Lease -ScopeId 10.20.30.0
explain: A scope has four parts: the network (`-ScopeAddress` + `-PrefixLength`), the pool range, the **options** (router, DNS, domain), and the state. A scope in state `Inactive` stores the config but hands out nothing.
Option 3 is the default router / gateway. Option 6 is DNS server. Option 15 is the DNS domain name. Setting only the pool is the classic beginner mistake.
A reservation needs the client's **MAC address** as `-ClientId`, not its hostname. `Get-NetNeighbor` or `arp -a` on the client gives it.
The scope address is the network address (all host bits zero) — `10.20.30.0` for a /24. Passing `10.20.30.1` will be rejected.
Verify by lease, not by assumption: `Get-DhcpServerv4Lease` proves a client actually took an address and shows what it was told.
example: A client gets an address but cannot resolve names: the scope exists and leases, but option 6 was never set. `Get-DhcpServerv4OptionValue -ScopeId 10.20.30.0` will show option 3 present and option 6 missing.

errors.message: Scope already exists
errors.means: A scope for that network is already present — possibly from a different server, which is a split-brain DHCP problem.
errors.fix: Get-DhcpServerv4Scope   # check which server holds it before deleting anything

errors.message: StartRange and EndRange must be within the scope
errors.means: The range falls outside the prefix, or includes the network/broadcast address.
errors.fix: For a /24, valid hosts are .1 to .254. Never make .0 or .255 part of the pool.

title: diskpart
task: Inspect, initialise, partition and format a disk from the command line
changes: Yes, irreversibly for the operations that write to a disk.
undo: There is no undo for `clean`, `convert`, or creating a partition over existing data. Confirm the disk number with `list disk` before every write operation.
risks: `clean`, `clean all` and `create partition` destroy data. Disk numbering is not stable across reboots on some hardware — re-run `list disk` every single time.
commands:
diskpart
list disk
select disk 2
detail disk
list partition
select partition 1
format fs=ntfs quick label=Data
assign letter=E
create partition primary
convert mbr
explain: The order matters and every step is verified before the next: `list disk` to see what is there, `select disk N`, `detail disk` to confirm you picked the right one by size and model, then act.
A disk shows as **Online** but uninitialised means it has raw capacity the OS refuses to touch until it gets an init record. `select disk N` then `initialize disk` fixes it.
MBR is a real limitation, not a preference: MBR partitions max at 2 TB and there can be at most four primary partitions. Anything larger needs GPT.
`format fs=ntfs quick` skips the zero pass. That is correct for a nearly empty disk and wrong as a data-wiping exercise — say which one you mean.
`list volume` and `list partition` are different views. A disk with no partition table shows a volume list with nothing on it.
example: A new 2 TB drive does not appear in File Explorer. `list disk` shows it as `Online`, 1863 GB, with no partitions. `initialize disk` then `convert gpt` then `create partition primary` then `format` and `assign` makes it appear.

errors.message: The media is write protected
errors.means: The device or a controller flag is preventing writes. Common on a USB stick with a physical lock, or a card reader.
errors.fix: Check the physical lock switch. A write-protected controller cannot be fixed in software.

errors.message: Virtual Disk Service error: The media is write protected / The disk is offline
errors.means: Windows has marked the disk offline, often because it believes it was removed uncleanly.
errors.fix: Set-Disk -Number N -IsOffline $false   # then re-run list disk

sources.title: Microsoft Learn — Initialize, format, and partition data disks

title: chkdsk
task: Check a volume for file-system errors and repair it
changes: Yes. Repairs the file system; /r also attempts to recover bad sectors.
undo: No. The changes are corrective repairs, not reversible edits.
risks: Running chkdsk on a volume with a synchronisation tool (ReFS with Storage Spaces, some databases, a File Replication Service member) can corrupt data. A scheduled chkdsk at boot while holding a volume lock can also fail.
commands:
chkdsk C: /scan
chkdsk D: /f
chkdsk E: /r
chkdsk D: /f /spotfix
explain: /scan is an online scan that needs no reboot and is safe to run while the volume is in use. It is the right first command.
/f fixes file-system errors. It requires the volume to be dismounted, so on the system volume it will offer to run at next boot.
/r adds a surface scan for bad sectors and can take hours on a large or failing disk. `/x` forces the dismount even when dirty, and is more disruptive than you usually want.
`/spotfix` queues a repair of what `/scan` found, to run at next boot. `/f /spotfix` together is the modern equivalent of the old scheduled chkdsk.
Before `/r` on a failing drive, image the disk first. Chkdsk can make recovery harder once it starts moving clusters around.
example: A drive that keeps saying 'found problems with the file system' at every boot: `chkdsk C: /scan` to confirm, then `chkdsk C: /f /spotfix` to repair at the next restart.

errors.message: Cannot lock current drive. Chkdsk was run because the volume may have been left dirty by an unclean shutdown.
errors.means: The OS has marked the volume dirty and wants to run offline. This is normal after a hard power-off.
errors.fix: Allow it to run at next boot, or run: chkdsk C: /f /spotfix

errors.message: Chkdsk is not available for RAW CD or DVD drives
errors.means: Optical media. Chkdsk applies to hard-disk volumes only.
errors.fix: n/a
